claim: Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory response to infection and a leading cause of death.
source: Sepsis is a systemic inflammatory response to infection and a leading cause of death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Singer et al., 2016 in the introduction.

claim: Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells are innate-like T cells enriched in mucosal tissues that recognize bacterial ligands.
source: Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells are innate-like T cells enriched in mucosal tissues that recognize bacterial ligands.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about MAIT cells.

claim: In experimental sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice had significantly increased mortality compared to wild-type mice.
source: In experimental sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice had significantly increased mortality and bacterial load, and reduced tissue-specific cytokine responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A where Mr1-/- mice had significantly increased sepsis-related mortality compared to WT mice (p=0.0007).

claim: MAIT-deficient mice had significantly increased bacterial load compared to wild-type mice in experimental sepsis.
source: In experimental sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice had significantly increased mortality and bacterial load, and reduced tissue-specific cytokine responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B where Mr1-/- mice had significantly higher bacterial burden in blood compared to WT mice.

claim: MAIT-deficient mice had reduced tissue-specific cytokine responses in experimental sepsis.
source: In experimental sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice had significantly increased mortality and bacterial load, and reduced tissue-specific cytokine responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 where Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-17A, IL-10, and GM-CSF compared to WT mice.

claim: MAIT cells of WT mice expressed lower levels of IFN-γ during sepsis compared to sham surgery.
source: MAIT cells of WT mice expressed lower levels of IFN-γ and IL-17a during sepsis compared to sham surgery, changes not seen in non-MAIT T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C (gene expression, p=0.04) and Figure 2A (protein expression, p=0.04).

claim: MAIT cells of WT mice expressed lower levels of IL-17a during sepsis compared to sham surgery.
source: MAIT cells of WT mice expressed lower levels of IFN-γ and IL-17a during sepsis compared to sham surgery, changes not seen in non-MAIT T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C where Il17a gene expression was significantly lower in septic mice compared to sham mice (p=0.02).

claim: Non-MAIT T cells did not show decreased IFN-γ and IL-17a expression during sepsis compared to sham surgery.
source: MAIT cells of WT mice expressed lower levels of IFN-γ and IL-17a during sepsis compared to sham surgery, changes not seen in non-MAIT T cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D where Ifng, Il17a, and Gzmb mRNA expression levels were similar between septic mice and sham mice in non-MAIT TCRβ+CD3+ T cell populations.

claim: MAIT cells of patients at sepsis presentation were significantly reduced in frequency compared to healthy donors.
source: MAIT cells of patients at sepsis presentation were significantly reduced in frequency compared to healthy donors, and were more activated, with decreased IFN-γ production, compared to both healthy donors and paired 90-day samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B where septic patients showed lower frequencies of MR1-tetramer+ MAIT cells compared to healthy donors.

claim: MAIT cells of patients at sepsis presentation were more activated compared to healthy donors.
source: MAIT cells of patients at sepsis presentation were significantly reduced in frequency compared to healthy donors, and were more activated, with decreased IFN-γ production, compared to both healthy donors and paired 90-day samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D where the expression of MAIT cell activation markers (CD69, CD38, and CD137) was significantly higher in septic patients compared to HD.

claim: MAIT cells of patients at sepsis presentation had decreased IFN-γ production compared to healthy donors.
source: MAIT cells of patients at sepsis presentation were significantly reduced in frequency compared to healthy donors, and were more activated, with decreased IFN-γ production, compared to both healthy donors and paired 90-day samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A where MAIT cells from septic patients showed significantly less IFN-γ production after E. coli stimulation compared with HD.

claim: MAIT cells of patients at sepsis presentation had decreased IFN-γ production compared to paired 90-day samples.
source: MAIT cells of patients at sepsis presentation were significantly reduced in frequency compared to healthy donors, and were more activated, with decreased IFN-γ production, compared to both healthy donors and paired 90-day samples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A where IFN-γ production returned to levels comparable with HD at Day 90.

claim: MAIT cells are highly activated and become dysfunctional during clinical sepsis.
source: Our data suggest that MAIT cells are highly activated and become dysfunctional during clinical sepsis, and contribute to tissue-specific cytokine responses that are protective against mortality during experimental sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased activation markers (Figure 6D) and decreased IFN-γ production (Figure 7A) in septic patients.

claim: MAIT cells contribute to tissue-specific cytokine responses that are protective against mortality during experimental sepsis.
source: Our data suggest that MAIT cells are highly activated and become dysfunctional during clinical sepsis, and contribute to tissue-specific cytokine responses that are protective against mortality during experimental sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that Mr1-/- mice had reduced lung cytokines (Figure 4) and increased mortality (Figure 3A).

claim: Sepsis accounts for 5.3 million deaths annually worldwide.
source: It is a leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for 5.3 million deaths annually (Fleischmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fleischmann et al., 2016.

claim: Sepsis is characterized by a systemic acute pathologic hyper-inflammatory response and an opposing anti-inflammatory response that can occur concurrently.
source: Sepsis is characterized by a systemic acute pathologic hyper-inflammatory response and an opposing anti-inflammatory response that can occur concurrently (Gentile et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gentile et al., 2012.

claim: Hallmarks of sepsis include a decreased ability to eliminate primary pathogens and an increased susceptibility to secondary nosocomial infections.
source: Hallmarks of sepsis include a decreased ability to eliminate primary pathogens and an increased susceptibility to secondary nosocomial infections (Otto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Otto et al., 2011.

claim: Sepsis is associated with a protracted immunosuppressed state that contributes to morbidity and mortality.
source: In addition, it is associated with a protracted immunosuppressed state that contributes to morbidity and mortality (Hotchkiss et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hotchkiss et al., 2013.

claim: Clinical trials over the past 3 decades of interventions targeting the hyper-inflammatory state of sepsis have largely failed to consistently improve clinical outcomes.
source: Unfortunately, clinical trials over the past 3 decades of interventions targeting the hyper-inflammatory state of sepsis have largely failed to consistently improve clinical outcomes (Cohen et al., 2012; PROWESS-SHOCK Study Group et al., 2012; Williams, 2012), and effective treatments are needed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2012; PROWESS-SHOCK Study Group et al., 2012; Williams, 2012.

claim: MAIT cells are restricted by MHC-related molecule 1 (MR1).
source: MAIT cells are innate-like T cells restricted by MHC-related molecule 1 (MR1) and MAIT ligands belong to a class of transitory intermediates of the riboflavin synthesis pathway (Porcelli et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Porcelli et al., 1993 and is established knowledge about MAIT cells.

claim: MAIT ligands belong to a class of transitory intermediates of the riboflavin synthesis pathway.
source: MAIT cells are innate-like T cells restricted by MHC-related molecule 1 (MR1) and MAIT ligands belong to a class of transitory intermediates of the riboflavin synthesis pathway (Porcelli et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Porcelli et al., 1993.

claim: MAIT cells express an invariant T cell receptor (TCR) TRAV1-2 (or Vα7.2) in humans.
source: They express an invariant T cell receptor (TCR) TRAV1-2 (or Vα7.2) in humans and TRAV-1 (or Vα19) in mice and a variable, but restricted, number of TRAJ and TCR β chains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAIT cells.

claim: MAIT cells express an invariant T cell receptor (TCR) TRAV-1 (or Vα19) in mice.
source: They express an invariant T cell receptor (TCR) TRAV1-2 (or Vα7.2) in humans and TRAV-1 (or Vα19) in mice and a variable, but restricted, number of TRAJ and TCR β chains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAIT cells.

claim: In humans, MAIT cells constitute 1–10% of peripheral blood T lymphocytes.
source: In humans, they constitute 1–10% of peripheral blood T lymphocytes, up to 10% of intestinal T cells, and up to 40% of T cells in the liver (Lee et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2009.

claim: In humans, MAIT cells constitute up to 10% of intestinal T cells.
source: In humans, they constitute 1–10% of peripheral blood T lymphocytes, up to 10% of intestinal T cells, and up to 40% of T cells in the liver (Lee et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2009.

claim: In humans, MAIT cells constitute up to 40% of T cells in the liver.
source: In humans, they constitute 1–10% of peripheral blood T lymphocytes, up to 10% of intestinal T cells, and up to 40% of T cells in the liver (Lee et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2009.

claim: Recent studies have highlighted the protective role of MAIT cells in host antibacterial responses in vivo.
source: Recent studies have highlighted the protective role of MAIT cells in host antibacterial responses in vivo (Georgel et al., 2011; Chua et al., 2012; Le Bourhis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Georgel et al., 2011; Chua et al., 2012; Le Bourhis et al., 2010.

claim: In patients with sepsis, MAIT cell frequencies are decreased in circulation compared to healthy control donors and uninfected critically-ill patients.
source: It has also been shown that in patients with sepsis, MAIT cell frequencies are decreased in circulation compared to healthy control donors and uninfected critically-ill patients (Grimaldi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grimaldi et al., 2014.

claim: Septic patients with persistent MAIT cell depletion have a higher incidence of secondary, ICU-acquired infections.
source: Septic patients with persistent MAIT cell depletion also have a higher incidence of secondary, ICU-acquired infections (Grimaldi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grimaldi et al., 2014.

claim: The frequencies of MR1-5OP-RU-tetramer+ MAIT cells in CLP mice were similar to those in sham mice.
source: While we noted similar frequencies of MR1-5OP-RU-tetramer+ (from here on, referred to as MR1-tetramer+) MAIT cells in CLP mice as in sham mice (Figure 1A and B), we found in sorted MAIT cells that gene expression of MAIT effectors Ifng (p=0.04) and Il17a (p=0.02) were significantly lower (and GzmB trended lower, p=0.14) in septic mice compared to sham mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gene expression of Ifng in MAIT cells was significantly lower in septic mice compared to sham mice (p=0.04).
source: While we noted similar frequencies of MR1-5OP-RU-tetramer+ (from here on, referred to as MR1-tetramer+) MAIT cells in CLP mice as in sham mice (Figure 1A and B), we found in sorted MAIT cells that gene expression of MAIT effectors Ifng (p=0.04) and Il17a (p=0.02) were significantly lower (and GzmB trended lower, p=0.14) in septic mice compared to sham mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gene expression of Il17a in MAIT cells was significantly lower in septic mice compared to sham mice (p=0.02).
source: While we noted similar frequencies of MR1-5OP-RU-tetramer+ (from here on, referred to as MR1-tetramer+) MAIT cells in CLP mice as in sham mice (Figure 1A and B), we found in sorted MAIT cells that gene expression of MAIT effectors Ifng (p=0.04) and Il17a (p=0.02) were significantly lower (and GzmB trended lower, p=0.14) in septic mice compared to sham mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gene expression of GzmB in MAIT cells trended lower in septic mice compared to sham mice (p=0.14).
source: While we noted similar frequencies of MR1-5OP-RU-tetramer+ (from here on, referred to as MR1-tetramer+) MAIT cells in CLP mice as in sham mice (Figure 1A and B), we found in sorted MAIT cells that gene expression of MAIT effectors Ifng (p=0.04) and Il17a (p=0.02) were significantly lower (and GzmB trended lower, p=0.14) in septic mice compared to sham mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In non-MAIT TCRβ+CD3+ T cell populations, Ifng, Il17a, and Gzmb mRNA expression levels were similar between septic mice and sham mice.
source: Conversely, in non-MAIT TCRβ+CD3+ T cell populations, Ifng (p=0.06), Il17a (p=0.16), and Gzmb (p=0.49) mRNA expression levels were similar between septic mice and sham mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Percentage frequencies of MAIT cells expressing IFNγ were significantly lower (p=0.04) in septic mice compared to sham mice.
source: We found that similar to Ifng mRNA expression, percentage frequencies of MAIT cells expressing IFNγ were significantly lower (p=0.04) in septic mice compared to sham mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) of IFNγ staining in TCRβ+ MR1-5OP-RU-tetramer+ MAIT cells was significantly reduced (p=0.02) in septic mice compared to sham mice.
source: The mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) of IFNγ staining in TCRβ+ MR1-5OP-RU-tetramer+ MAIT cells was also significantly reduced (p=0.02) in septic mice compared to sham mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In non-MAIT TCRβ+CD3+ T cell populations, IFNγ protein expression was significantly higher (p=0.0005) in septic mice compared to sham mice.
source: Conversely, in non-MAIT TCRβ+CD3+ T cell populations, IFNγ protein expression was significantly higher (p=0.0005) in septic mice compared to sham mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No significant differences were observed in IFNγ expression in iNKT and TCRγδ cells between septic and sham mice.
source: No significant differences were observed in IFNγ expression in iNKT and TCRγδ cells (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: MR1-deficient mice (Mr1-/-) lack MAIT cells.
source: We examined whether the absence of MAIT cells altered survival outcomes in vivo during experimental sepsis. In the CLP model of polymicrobial sepsis (Yost et al., 2016; Middleton et al., 2019), we saw that MR1-deficient mice (Mr1-/-) which lack MAIT cells, had significantly increased sepsis-related mortality compared to WT mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Mr1-/- mice.

claim: The majority (11/15,~73%) of Mr1-/- mice died 24 to 48 hr following induction of sepsis.
source: The majority (11/15,~73%) of Mr1-/- mice died 24 to 48 hr following induction of sepsis, while the majority (13/15,~87%) of WT mice survived up to 100 hr after sepsis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The majority (13/15,~87%) of WT mice survived up to 100 hr after sepsis.
source: The majority (11/15,~73%) of Mr1-/- mice died 24 to 48 hr following induction of sepsis, while the majority (13/15,~87%) of WT mice survived up to 100 hr after sepsis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mr1-/- mice had a significantly higher burden of bacteria in blood compared to WT mice 18 hr following CLP.
source: On examining the bacterial counts 18 hr following CLP, we found that Mr1-/- mice had a significantly higher burden of bacteria in blood compared to WT mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In experiments with bedding transfer between Mr1-/- and WT cages prior to CLP, Mr1-/- mice had significantly increased mortality compared to WT mice.
source: In experiments in which bedding was transferred between Mr1-/- and WT cages (Miyoshi et al., 2018) prior to CLP, we found that Mr1-/- mice had significantly increased mortality compared to WT mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mr1-/- mice had significantly higher mortality from ExPEC sepsis compared to WT mice.
source: As we observed in the CLP, polymicrobial model of sepsis, Mr1-/- mice had significantly higher mortality from ExPEC sepsis, compared to WT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IFN-γ following CLP.
source: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-17A, IL-10, and GM-CSF: cytokines produced by MAIT cells (Xiao and Cai, 2017; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung TNFα following CLP.
source: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-17A, IL-10, and GM-CSF: cytokines produced by MAIT cells (Xiao and Cai, 2017; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IL-17A following CLP.
source: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-17A, IL-10, and GM-CSF: cytokines produced by MAIT cells (Xiao and Cai, 2017; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IL-10 following CLP.
source: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-17A, IL-10, and GM-CSF: cytokines produced by MAIT cells (Xiao and Cai, 2017; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung GM-CSF following CLP.
source: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-17A, IL-10, and GM-CSF: cytokines produced by MAIT cells (Xiao and Cai, 2017; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-17A, IL-10, and GM-CSF are cytokines produced by MAIT cells.
source: Compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had significantly reduced levels of lung IFN-γ, TNFα, IL-17A, IL-10, and GM-CSF: cytokines produced by MAIT cells (Xiao and Cai, 2017; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xiao and Cai, 2017.

claim: Serum, liver, and gut cytokines were less affected than lung cytokines in Mr1-/- mice following sepsis.
source: Interestingly, serum, liver, and gut cytokines were less affected than lung cytokines in Mr1-/- mice following sepsis (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: As compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had a significantly lower proportion of interstitial macrophages (IMs) following CLP.
source: As compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had a significantly lower proportion of IMs (Siglec-F-, CD24-, MHCII+, CD11c+, CD11b+, CD64+ cells; Figure 5A) and moDCs (Siglec-F-, MHCII+, CD11c+, CD11b+, Ly-6C+ cells; Figure 5B) following CLP.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: As compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had a significantly lower proportion of monocytic dendritic cells (moDCs) following CLP.
source: As compared to WT mice, Mr1-/- mice had a significantly lower proportion of IMs (Siglec-F-, CD24-, MHCII+, CD11c+, CD11b+, CD64+ cells; Figure 5A) and moDCs (Siglec-F-, MHCII+, CD11c+, CD11b+, Ly-6C+ cells; Figure 5B) following CLP.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The loss of MAIT cells did not influence alveolar macrophages (AMs) following CLP.
source: The loss of MAIT cells did not influence AMs, pDCs, or neutrophils, however, following CLP (Figure 5C -E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The loss of MAIT cells did not influence plasmocytoid DCs (pDCs) following CLP.
source: The loss of MAIT cells did not influence AMs, pDCs, or neutrophils, however, following CLP (Figure 5C -E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The loss of MAIT cells did not influence neutrophils following CLP.
source: The loss of MAIT cells did not influence AMs, pDCs, or neutrophils, however, following CLP (Figure 5C -E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Co-cultures of lung MAIT cells with Ly6C+ CD11b+ monocytes stimulated with 5-A-RU and MeG produced significantly higher amounts of IFNγ compared to unstimulated and monocyte only controls.
source: We found significantly higher amounts of IFNγ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and GM-CSF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) in co-cultures stimulated with 5-amino-6-D-ribitylaminouracil (5-A-RU) and methylglyoxal (MeG) (Li et al., 2018) compared to unstimulated and monocyte only controls indicating that MAIT cells in the lung can interact with monocytes to produce effector cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Co-cultures of lung MAIT cells with Ly6C+ CD11b+ monocytes stimulated with 5-A-RU and MeG produced significantly higher amounts of GM-CSF compared to unstimulated and monocyte only controls.
source: We found significantly higher amounts of IFNγ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and GM-CSF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) in co-cultures stimulated with 5-amino-6-D-ribitylaminouracil (5-A-RU) and methylglyoxal (MeG) (Li et al., 2018) compared to unstimulated and monocyte only controls indicating that MAIT cells in the lung can interact with monocytes to produce effector cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MAIT cells in the lung can interact with monocytes to produce effector cytokines.
source: We found significantly higher amounts of IFNγ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and GM-CSF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) in co-cultures stimulated with 5-amino-6-D-ribitylaminouracil (5-A-RU) and methylglyoxal (MeG) (Li et al., 2018) compared to unstimulated and monocyte only controls indicating that MAIT cells in the lung can interact with monocytes to produce effector cytokines.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-culture experiment results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The frequencies of iNKT cells in the lungs were reduced during sepsis.
source: We observed that the frequencies of iNKT and γδ T cells in the lungs were reduced during sepsis, consistent with prior studies showing that frequencies of iNKT (Hu et al., 2009; Heffernan et al., 2013) and γδ T cells (Andreu-Ballester et al., 2013; Hirsh et al., 2004) are modulated in response to polymicrobial sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and citations to Hu et al., 2009; Heffernan et al., 2013.

claim: The frequencies of γδ T cells in the lungs were reduced during sepsis.
source: We observed that the frequencies of iNKT and γδ T cells in the lungs were reduced during sepsis, consistent with prior studies showing that frequencies of iNKT (Hu et al., 2009; Heffernan et al., 2013) and γδ T cells (Andreu-Ballester et al., 2013; Hirsh et al., 2004) are modulated in response to polymicrobial sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and citations to Andreu-Ballester et al., 2013; Hirsh et al., 2004.

claim: There were no differences in the frequencies of iNKT cells between Mr1-/- and WT mice.
source: However, there were no differences in the frequencies of iNKT or γδ T cells between Mr1-/- and WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There were no differences in the frequencies of γδ T cells between Mr1-/- and WT mice.
source: However, there were no differences in the frequencies of iNKT or γδ T cells between Mr1-/- and WT mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The study examined MAIT cells from 33 septic patients within 48 (±24) hr of ICU admission for sepsis.
source: We examined MAIT cells isolated from the blood of 33 septic patients (16 female and 17 male, mean age 59 + / - 2.7 years, mean SOFA score 4.6) within 48 (±24) hr of ICU admission for sepsis (day 1, D1).
evidence: This describes the patient cohort studied.

claim: In 12 septic patients, MAIT phenotyping was repeated approximately 90 days after their ICU admission for sepsis.
source: In 12 of these same patients (6 female and 6 male, mean age 60.5 + / - 4 years), we repeated MAIT phenotyping again approximately 90 days after their ICU admission for sepsis.
evidence: This describes the longitudinal follow-up of a subset of patients.

claim: The study compared septic patients to 21 age- and sex-matched healthy donors.
source: We compared them to 21 age- and sex-matched healthy donors (HD) (10 female and 11 male, mean age 51 + / - 3.8 years).
evidence: This describes the control group.

claim: Upon ICU admission, septic patients showed lower frequencies of MR1-tetramer+ MAIT cells within the T cell (CD3+) compartment compared to healthy donors.
source: Upon ICU admission, septic patients showed lower frequencies of MR1-tetramer+ MAIT cells within the T cell (CD3+) compartment compared to healthy donors (HD) (Figure 6, A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At 90 days after sepsis, MAIT cell frequencies were not statistically different from Day 1 septic patients and healthy donors.
source: At 90 days after sepsis, MAIT cell frequencies were not statistically different from Day 1 septic patients and HD (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Upon ICU admission (Day 1), the expression of MAIT cell activation markers CD69, CD38, and CD137 was significantly higher in septic patients compared to healthy donors.
source: Upon ICU admission (Day 1), the expression of MAIT cell activation markers, including CD69, CD38, and CD137, was significantly higher in septic patients compared to HD (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When assessed on Day 90, the expression of MAIT cell activation markers had returned to levels comparable to healthy donors.
source: However, when assessed again in these same septic patients on Day 90, the expression of MAIT cell activation markers had returned to levels comparable to HD (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Upon ICU admission, there was a higher expression of TIM-3 (p=0.03) in MAIT cells of septic patients compared to healthy donors.
source: Upon ICU admission, we also found a higher expression of TIM-3 (p=0.03), and LAG-3 (trend with p=0.14), inhibitory receptors associated with T cell exhaustion, in MAIT cells of septic patients compared to HD (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Upon ICU admission, there was a trend toward higher expression of LAG-3 (p=0.14) in MAIT cells of septic patients compared to healthy donors.
source: Upon ICU admission, we also found a higher expression of TIM-3 (p=0.03), and LAG-3 (trend with p=0.14), inhibitory receptors associated with T cell exhaustion, in MAIT cells of septic patients compared to HD (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Exhaustion markers LAG-3 and TIM-3 in septic patients at Day 90 had returned to levels similar to that of healthy donors.
source: As with MAIT cell activation markers, exhaustion markers LAG-3 and TIM-3 in septic patients at Day 90 had returned to levels similar to that of HD (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: PD-1 expression was lower (but not statistically significant, p=0.11) in septic patients compared to healthy donors.
source: Of note, PD-1 expression was lower (but not statistically significant, p=0.11) in septic patients compared to HD (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Upon ICU admission, MAIT cells from septic patients showed significantly less IFN-γ production after E. coli stimulation compared with healthy donors.
source: Upon ICU admission, MAIT cells from septic patients showed significantly less IFN-γ production after E. coli stimulation, compared with HD. As with MAIT cell activation and exhaustion markers, IFN-γ production returned to levels comparable with HD at Day 90 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: IFN-γ production by MAIT cells returned to levels comparable with healthy donors at Day 90.
source: Upon ICU admission, MAIT cells from septic patients showed significantly less IFN-γ production after E. coli stimulation, compared with HD. As with MAIT cell activation and exhaustion markers, IFN-γ production returned to levels comparable with HD at Day 90 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No significant differences were observed in IL-17 expression in MAIT cells among the groups (healthy donors, Day 1 sepsis, Day 90 sepsis).
source: No significant differences were observed in IL-17 (Figure 7B), TNF-α (Figure 7C), and granzyme B (Figure 7D) expression in MAIT cells among the groups.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: No significant differences were observed in TNF-α expression in MAIT cells among the groups (healthy donors, Day 1 sepsis, Day 90 sepsis).
source: No significant differences were observed in IL-17 (Figure 7B), TNF-α (Figure 7C), and granzyme B (Figure 7D) expression in MAIT cells among the groups.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No significant differences were observed in granzyme B expression in MAIT cells among the groups (healthy donors, Day 1 sepsis, Day 90 sepsis).
source: No significant differences were observed in IL-17 (Figure 7B), TNF-α (Figure 7C), and granzyme B (Figure 7D) expression in MAIT cells among the groups.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: During clinical sepsis, MAIT cell frequencies are lower, highly activated, and less capable of mounting IFN-γ responses upon stimulation.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that during clinical sepsis, MAIT cell frequencies are lower, highly activated, and less capable of mounting IFN-γ responses upon stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: At 90 days following sepsis, MAIT cell activation and IFN-γ responses have returned to levels comparable with matched healthy donors.
source: Moreover, at 90 days following sepsis, MAIT cell activation and IFN-γ responses have returned to levels comparable with matched HD.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: MAIT cells play an important role in antibacterial responses.
source: Recent reports provide evidence that MAIT cells play an important role in antibacterial responses (Le Bourhis et al., 2010; Ghazarian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Le Bourhis et al., 2010; Ghazarian et al., 2017.

claim: Acutely during clinical sepsis, MAIT cells are highly activated, lower in frequency, and have an altered functional phenotype evidenced by reduced IFN-γ cytokine expression.
source: We show that acutely during clinical sepsis, MAIT cells are highly activated, lower in frequency, and have an altered functional phenotype evidenced by reduced IFN-γ cytokine expression.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: At 90 days after sepsis, changes in MAIT cells have resolved as compared to matched healthy subjects.
source: Moreover, at 90 days after sepsis, these changes in MAIT cells have resolved as compared to matched healthy subjects.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Tissue-resident MAIT cells are dysfunctional during sepsis.
source: Using relevant animal models of sepsis, we show similarly that tissue-resident MAIT cells are dysfunctional during sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1 and 2 showing decreased effector function.

claim: MAIT cells are protective during sepsis.
source: Moreover, our experimental data indicate that MAIT cells are protective during sepsis, as a deficiency of MAIT cells resulted in significantly higher bacterial burden and mortality.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 showing increased mortality and bacterial burden in Mr1-/- mice.

claim: Despite being rendered dysfunctional, MAIT cells may augment host immune responses and therefore outcomes during sepsis.
source: These results indicate that despite being rendered dysfunctional, MAIT cells may augment host immune responses and therefore outcomes during sepsis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined findings of MAIT cell dysfunction and protective effects.

claim: The differences in mortality observed with CLP are unlikely to be due to differences in the microbiota.
source: Our experimental data from the ExPEC model of sepsis, as well as from experiments where bedding was transferred between Mr1-/- and WT mice, suggest that the differences in mortality observed with CLP are unlikely to be due to differences in the microbiota.
evidence: This is inferred from the bedding transfer experiments (Figure 3C) and ExPEC experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: MAIT cells play a protective role against sepsis pathology by regulating cytokine expression and maintaining a balance in immune response following sepsis to minimize tissue injury.
source: We hypothesize that MAIT cells play a protective role against sepsis pathology by regulating cytokine expression and maintaining a balance in immune response following sepsis to minimize tissue injury.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed data.

claim: MAIT cells are capable of bridging the innate and adaptive immune systems.
source: As MAIT cells are capable of bridging the innate and adaptive immune systems, it has also been postulated that their actions are mediated in part by their interaction with macrophages or monocyte-derived dendritic cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAIT cells.

claim: In sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice produce less GM-CSF compared to WT mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that in sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice produce less GM-CSF and have lower frequencies of lung interstitial macrophages and monocytic dendritic cells compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4E.

claim: In sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice have lower frequencies of lung interstitial macrophages compared to WT mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that in sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice produce less GM-CSF and have lower frequencies of lung interstitial macrophages and monocytic dendritic cells compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: In sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice have lower frequencies of lung monocytic dendritic cells compared to WT mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that in sepsis, MAIT-deficient mice produce less GM-CSF and have lower frequencies of lung interstitial macrophages and monocytic dendritic cells compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: MAIT cells promote early pulmonary GM-CSF production during pulmonary infection.
source: These observations are concordant with previous work demonstrating MAIT cell promotion of early pulmonary GM-CSF production, and differentiation of inflammatory monocytes into moDCs during pulmonary infection (Meierovics and Cowley, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meierovics and Cowley, 2016.

claim: MAIT cells promote differentiation of inflammatory monocytes into moDCs during pulmonary infection.
source: These observations are concordant with previous work demonstrating MAIT cell promotion of early pulmonary GM-CSF production, and differentiation of inflammatory monocytes into moDCs during pulmonary infection (Meierovics and Cowley, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meierovics and Cowley, 2016.

claim: MAIT cells are decreased in patients with severe sepsis.
source: Our finding of decreased MAIT cell frequencies during severe sepsis are consistent with a previous study demonstrating that MAIT cells are decreased in patients with severe sepsis, a decrease that was not seen in other T cell populations examined, including iNKT and γδ T cells, suggesting cell-specific, rather than global, depletion (Grimaldi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grimaldi et al., 2014.

claim: The decrease in MAIT cells during sepsis was not seen in other T cell populations examined, including iNKT and γδ T cells, suggesting cell-specific, rather than global, depletion.
source: Our finding of decreased MAIT cell frequencies during severe sepsis are consistent with a previous study demonstrating that MAIT cells are decreased in patients with severe sepsis, a decrease that was not seen in other T cell populations examined, including iNKT and γδ T cells, suggesting cell-specific, rather than global, depletion (Grimaldi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grimaldi et al., 2014.

claim: At approximately 90 days after sepsis, MAIT cell frequencies had returned to similar levels observed in matched healthy donors.
source: To extend this work, we found that at approximately 90 days after sepsis MAIT cell frequencies had returned to similar levels observed in matched healthy donors.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: MAIT cells express elevated levels of activation markers in septic patients.
source: Furthermore, we found that MAIT cells express elevated levels of activation markers in septic patients and that these markers also return to similar levels as in healthy donors following recovery from sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: MAIT cell activation markers return to similar levels as in healthy donors following recovery from sepsis.
source: Furthermore, we found that MAIT cells express elevated levels of activation markers in septic patients and that these markers also return to similar levels as in healthy donors following recovery from sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6D.

claim: The depletion of MAIT cells from circulation in septic patients may be a result of apoptotic cell death, TCR internalization, or migration to peripheral tissues.
source: The depletion of MAIT cells from circulation in septic patients is similar to what has been observed in other infections (Leeansyah et al., 2013; Shaler et al., 2017; Leung et al., 2014), and may be a result of apoptotic cell death, TCR internalization, or migration to peripheral tissues, although the underlying mechanisms remain to be elucidated.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations in other infections cited (Leeansyah et al., 2013; Shaler et al., 2017; Leung et al., 2014).

claim: A previous study showed an association between MAIT cell frequency and protection against secondary infection in the ICU.
source: A previous study had shown an association between MAIT cell frequency and protection against secondary infection in the ICU (Grimaldi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grimaldi et al., 2014.

claim: In D1 sepsis patients, ex vivo stimulated MAIT cells had a depressed IFN-γ response compared to healthy donors and patients reassessed 90 days following admission for sepsis.
source: In this study, we found that in D1 sepsis patients, ex vivo stimulated MAIT cells had a depressed IFN-γ response compared to healthy donors and patients reassessed 90 days following admission for sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7A.

claim: A similar decrease in IFN-γ response was seen in MAIT cells in the lung tissue of mice undergoing CLP compared to mice undergoing sham surgery.
source: A similar decrease in IFN-γ response was also seen in MAIT cells in the lung tissue of mice undergoing CLP compared to mice undergoing sham surgery.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: During clinical sepsis, MAIT cells are dysfunctional.
source: Together with an increase in expression of co-inhibitory receptors on human MAIT cells, our data suggest that during clinical sepsis, MAIT cells are dysfunctional.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing increased co-inhibitory receptors (Figure 6E) and decreased IFN-γ production (Figure 7A).

claim: MAIT cell dysfunction may prevent MAIT cells from mounting an optimal response against microbial pathogens.
source: This may prevent MAIT cells from mounting an optimal response against microbial pathogens, a hypothesis consistent with our experimental data indicating that the loss of MAIT cells results in increased bacterial burden and mortality during sepsis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed dysfunction and experimental data from Mr1-/- mice.

claim: Superantigens from bacterial pathogens such as Staphylococcus spp. and Streptococcus spp. can directly trigger rapid activation of MAIT cells to mount IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-2 responses in an MR1-independent manner.
source: Previous work has shown that superantigens from bacterial pathogens such as Staphylococcus spp. and Streptococcus spp. can directly trigger rapid activation of MAIT cells to mount IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-2 responses in an MR1-independent manner (Shaler et al., 2017), and that MAIT cells primed by superantigens are exhausted and anergic to cognate antigens such as E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shaler et al., 2017.

claim: MAIT cells primed by superantigens are exhausted and anergic to cognate antigens such as E. coli.
source: Previous work has shown that superantigens from bacterial pathogens such as Staphylococcus spp. and Streptococcus spp. can directly trigger rapid activation of MAIT cells to mount IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-2 responses in an MR1-independent manner (Shaler et al., 2017), and that MAIT cells primed by superantigens are exhausted and anergic to cognate antigens such as E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shaler et al., 2017.

claim: MAIT cells undergo functional and phenotypic changes during clinical and experimental sepsis.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrate that MAIT cells undergo functional and phenotypic changes during clinical and experimental sepsis.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MAIT deficient mice have a higher microbial burden during sepsis.
source: We found that MAIT deficient mice have a higher microbial burden, lower tissue cytokine production, and higher mortality during sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: MAIT deficient mice have lower tissue cytokine production during sepsis.
source: We found that MAIT deficient mice have a higher microbial burden, lower tissue cytokine production, and higher mortality during sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: MAIT deficient mice have higher mortality during sepsis.
source: We found that MAIT deficient mice have a higher microbial burden, lower tissue cytokine production, and higher mortality during sepsis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: MAIT cells contribute toward tissue-specific cytokine responses during sepsis.
source: Despite this dysfunction, our data provide new insights into the potential protective role of MAIT cells, and their contribution toward tissue-specific cytokine responses, during sepsis.
evidence: This is inferred from data showing reduced tissue cytokines in Mr1-/- mice (Figure 4).

claim: Defining MAIT cells as a critical therapeutic target during sepsis will potentially enable the development of novel translational strategies targeted to enhance MAIT cell functionality to improve outcomes in sepsis.
source: Defining MAIT cells as a critical therapeutic target during sepsis, and defining the mechanisms that regulate MAIT cell function, will potentially enable the development of novel translational strategies targeted to enhance MAIT cell functionality to improve outcomes in sepsis.
evidence: This is speculation about future therapeutic applications.

claim: MAIT cells can contribute to cytokine release from macrophages.
source: MAIT cells can contribute to cytokine release from macrophages (Hegde et al., 2018) and have shown to promote inflammatory monocyte differentiation into dendritic cells during pulmonary infection (Meierovics and Cowley, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hegde et al., 2018.

claim: The lung is among the most abundant site of MAIT cells in mice.
source: We chose lungs given the frequent association of lung injury with clinical sepsis (Fein et al., 1983; Martin et al., 2003), and because it is among the most abundant site of MAIT cells in mice (Rahimpour et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rahimpour et al., 2015.

claim: There is a frequent association of lung injury with clinical sepsis.
source: We chose lungs given the frequent association of lung injury with clinical sepsis (Fein et al., 1983; Martin et al., 2003), and because it is among the most abundant site of MAIT cells in mice (Rahimpour et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fein et al., 1983; Martin et al., 2003.
